text: Describe the embryological and anatomical divisions of the central nervous system (telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, myelencephalon, spinal cord).
Identify the lobes of the brain (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, limbic, insula) and the anatomical landmarks of primary gyri and sulci (central, lateral, parieto-occipital, calcarine).
Correlate cerebral cortical lobes with their primary specialized functions and clinical deficit syndromes (motor, sensory, visual, auditory, receptive/expressive language, executive).

Describe the internal architectural organization of the cerebrum, including gray matter (cortex, deep basal nuclei) and white matter tracts (corpus callosum, internal capsule anterior/posterior limbs, corona radiata).
Identify the gross external landmarks and divisions of the brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata) and their cranial nerve emergence points.

Describe the cranial meningeal layers (dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater), the intracranial dural reflections (falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli), and the pathology of intracranial hemorrhages (epidural, subdural, subarachnoid).
Detail the embryological stages of primary and secondary neurulation, identifying the derivatives of neuroectoderm, surface ectoderm, and neural crest cells.
Map the 3 primary brain vesicles (prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon) to the 5 secondary vesicles and their corresponding adult CNS and ventricular structures.
Explain the dorsal-ventral patterning of the neural tube guided by SHH and BMP, distinguishing the alar plate (sensory) from the basal plate (motor) separated by the sulcus limitans.

Describe the cellular mechanics of cortical development (radial glial scaffolding, inside-out neuronal migration) and disorders of proliferation/migration (microcephaly, lissencephaly, pachygyria, heterotopias).

Diagnose and differentiate neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele, encephalocele), including maternal serum AFP and acetylcholinesterase diagnostics, and folic acid prevention.

Contrast Arnold-Chiari Malformation Type I (isolated cerebellar tonsillar herniation, adult onset, syringomyelia association) with Type II (tonsillar and vermian herniation, congenital myelomeningocele, hydrocephalus).

Identify the clinical and radiological hallmarks of Dandy-Walker malformation (agenesis/hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis, cystic fourth ventricle enlargement, posterior fossa enlargement) and Holoprosencephaly (failure of hemispheric cleavage, SHH mutation, trisomy 13).
Differentiate autosomal recessive and X-linked sphingolipidoses by enzyme defect, accumulated lipid substrate, and systemic vs neurodegenerative clinical features.

Contrast Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A defect, GM2 ganglioside accumulation, hyperreflexia, cherry-red spot, onion-skin lysosomes, NO hepatosplenomegaly) with Niemann-Pick disease (sphingomyelinase defect, hepatosplenomegaly, foamy histiocytes).
Describe the clinical presentation and histology of Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase defect, hepatosplenomegaly, avascular bone necrosis, lipid-laden macrophages with crumpled paper cytoplasm).

Recognize the manifestations of Fabry disease (X-linked recessive, alpha-galactosidase A defect, ceramide trihexoside accumulation, acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, progressive renal/cardiac failure), Krabbe disease, and Metachromatic leukodystrophy.
Explain the biophysical basis of the neuronal resting membrane potential (-70 mV), K+ equilibrium potential, leak potassium conductances, and the electrogenic action of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump.

Detail the gating kinetics of voltage-gated Na+ channels (activation gate, inactivation gate) and voltage-gated K+ channels throughout the action potential, defining the absolute and relative refractory periods.

Explain factors influencing conduction velocity, including axonal diameter (internal longitudinal resistance), myelination (decreased membrane capacitance, increased membrane resistance), and saltatory conduction at nodes of Ranvier.

Describe the pharmacological mechanism of local anesthetics (blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels from the intracellular cytoplasmic side), state-dependence (preference for inactivated/open channels), and nerve fiber susceptibility (small/myelinated > unmyelinated > large motor).

Classify local anesthetics into esters (metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase; e.g., procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine) and amides (metabolized by hepatic CYP450; two 'i's: lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, mepivacaine).

Explain the impact of tissue pH on local anesthetic bioavailability (acidic infected tissue shifts equilibrium toward ionized form, reducing tissue penetration) and the rationale/contraindications of epinephrine co-administration.

Identify local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST: metallic taste, perioral paresthesias, seizures, cardiotoxicity/arrhythmias with bupivacaine) and immediate resuscitation with 20% intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid).

Delineate the molecular steps of synaptic transmission: depolarization, presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ influx (N- and P/Q-type channels), SNARE complex-mediated vesicle fusion (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25), exocytosis, and reuptake/recycling.

Contrast ionotropic (AMPA, NMDA, kainate) and metabotropic glutamate receptors, detailing the voltage-dependent Mg2+ block of NMDA receptors, Ca2+ permeability, synaptic plasticity, and glutamate excitotoxicity.

Describe inhibitory neurotransmission: GABA-A receptors (ionotropic Cl- channels, modulated by benzodiazepines, barbiturates, ethanol, z-drugs), GABA-B receptors (G-protein coupled K+ activation, baclofen), and glycine receptors.

Identify the primary central synthesis pathways, rate-limiting enzymes, and anatomical origins of monoamines: Dopamine (VTA, Substantia nigra), Norepinephrine (Locus coeruleus), Serotonin (Raphe nuclei), and Acetylcholine (Basal nucleus of Meynert).
Identify the structural components of neurons (soma, dendrites, axon hillock, axon, Nissl substance/rough ER) and mechanisms of anterograde (kinesin) and retrograde (dynein) axonal transport.

text: Characterize the histological features and physiological roles of CNS glial cells: Astrocytes (GFAP+, K+ buffering, neurotransmitter recycling, blood-brain barrier maintenance, reactive gliosis), Oligodendrocytes (myelinating multiple CNS axons), Microglia (mesodermal origin, phagocytosis), and Ependymal cells.

text: Contrast PNS Schwann cells (myelinating a single internode of one axon, promoting axonal regeneration) with CNS oligodendrocytes (inhibiting axonal regeneration via Nogo proteins).

text: Trace the pathway of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow from choroid plexus synthesis through the ventricular chambers, foramina (Monro, Sylvian aqueduct, Luschka, Magendie), subarachnoid space, and venous drainage via arachnoid granulations.
Differentiate communicating (non-obstructive) vs non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus by etiology, lumbar puncture opening pressure, and ventricular dilatation patterns.

Recognize the clinical presentation and neuroimaging of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH: classic wet, wacky, wobbly triad of urinary incontinence, cognitive decline, magnetic gait) and response to high-volume CSF tap or VP shunt.

Distinguish Hydrocephalus ex vacuo (compensatory ventricular enlargement due to cortical neurodegenerative atrophy) and Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri: elevated ICP, papilledema, normal ventricles, empty sella).
Diagnose acute cerebral herniation syndromes (subfalcine/ACA compression; uncal/ipsilateral CN III blown pupil, contralateral PCA stroke, Duret hemorrhage; tonsillar/fatal respiratory arrest).

Explain the physiological mechanisms of medical interventions for elevated intracranial pressure: head-of-bed elevation, therapeutic hyperventilation (hypocapnia-induced vasoconstriction), and hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol, hypertonic saline).

Contrast Myasthenia Gravis (post-synaptic AChR autoantibodies, fatiguing muscle weakness with use, ptosis/diplopia, thymoma association) with Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (pre-synaptic P/Q-type VGCC antibodies, weakness improving with use, autonomic dysfunction, hyporeflexia, small cell lung cancer association).

Explain the mechanism of Botulinum neurotoxin (cleavage of SNARE proteins synaptobrevin/SNAP-25 preventing presynaptic ACh exocytosis) and its clinical presentation (descending flaccid paralysis, cranial neuropathies, mydriasis, infant botulism).

Detail the pharmacokinetics and clinical applications of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine, neostigmine, edrophonium, physostigmine, donepezil), distinguishing quaternary amines (peripherally acting) from tertiary amines (CNS-penetrating).

Differentiate a Myasthenic Crisis (under-medication, respiratory failure, improves with AChE-I) from a Cholinergic Crisis (excessive AChE-I, depolarizing paralysis, muscarinic excess; managed by stopping AChE-I and administering atropine).

Recognize the toxidrome of organophosphate and nerve agent poisoning (irreversible AChE phosphorylation, DUMBBELSS muscarinic toxicity and nicotinic weakness) and its emergency management (Atropine for muscarinic blockade, Pralidoxime/2-PAM for AChE reactivation before enzyme aging).
